QF.id: XIII Introduction to the Underlying Markets_37

question.text: What is the significance of the 'benchmark' government security (on-the-run security) in the Indian bond market?

answer.text: It is the most recently issued and actively traded government security for a particular maturity, used as the reference for pricing other securities
It is the government bond with the highest coupon rate in the market
It is a special bond that can only be purchased by the Reserve Bank of India
It is a bond that has been outstanding for the longest period of time

explanation.text: The Logic: In sovereign bond markets, the "on-the-run" or benchmark government security for a given maturity bucket (most commonly the 10-year) is the most recently issued bond at that tenor. Because it is the freshest issue, it tends to trade with the highest secondary-market liquidity and tightest bid-ask spreads, which is why market participants use its yield as the reference rate for pricing other bonds, swaps, and rate derivatives at that tenor. The Trap: The benchmark is defined by recency and liquidity, not by having the highest coupon, by being RBI-restricted, or by being the oldest outstanding bond. Older issues at the same maturity are typically called "off-the-run" and trade less actively than the current benchmark. Note: The specific "most recently issued and actively traded" / on-the-run definition was not found in the cited Series IV workbook pages (p.20, p.82, p.83). The framing above is general fixed-income market knowledge about how on-the-run benchmarks operate in sovereign bond markets, not a workbook citation.
